title: How does prisoner tagging work?
summary: An electronic tag can help check conditions such as a curfew after release from prison. The same monitoring service is also used for court orders and immigration bail.

monitoring-process.title: From a monitoring condition to a response

steps.label: Set the condition
steps.text: The relevant authority sets the monitoring requirement and specifies what the person must do.

steps.label: Fit and activate the equipment
steps.text: The provider fits the tag and installs any other equipment needed. For prison leavers, that has usually meant a visit to their accommodation after release. The prison pilot fits tags before people leave.

steps.label: Monitor the condition
steps.text: The equipment checks the specified condition, such as a curfew, location restriction or alcohol requirement. The monitoring service reviews possible breaches.

steps.label: Assess and respond to an alert
steps.text: The monitoring service passes on suspected breaches when required. Probation handles responses to release-licence breaches, while police assess suspected breaches of electronically monitored court bail.

by-order.title: People assigned electronic monitoring equipment
by-order.note: The total includes all published order groups, including a small number in the immigration group who live in Scotland or Northern Ireland. The Ministry of Justice advises against comparing the figures with publications issued before June 2025 because the definition and counting method changed. The figures predate the release changes that began on 1 October 2026.

status-by-stage.title: Who had equipment, and was it sending a signal?
status-by-stage.description: Two snapshots of people with an active monitoring order in England and Wales. Each bar shows the share of everyone in that group at the date shown.
status-by-stage.note: Shares are rounded. A signal means the monitoring system received a communication in the previous 14 days. The post-release group includes people recorded as being back in custody. The Ministry removed additional expired court bail orders in September, which affected the recorded change for that group.

post-release-trend.title: People counted in the post-release monitoring caseload
post-release-trend.description: England and Wales, at month end. Counts rose within the current series before falling from 10,924 in July to 10,290 in September 2026.
post-release-trend.note: July to September 2026 figures are provisional. The October 2026 release reforms began after the latest observation.

gps-reoffending.title: Proven reoffending in the GPS pilot
gps-reoffending.note: The evaluation estimated a seven percentage point reduction for men in the pilot. It matched eligible prison leavers on recorded characteristics, so differences the study could not measure may still affect the result.

gps-compliance.title: Recorded probation compliance in the GPS pilot
gps-compliance.note: This measures outcomes from recorded probation contacts. The difference was statistically uncertain. Separate analyses also found no clear difference in formal warnings for licence breaches or recall to prison.

purpose.text: After prison, tagging helps probation check whether someone follows conditions such as a curfew or staying away from a specified area. It is intended to support supervision in the community, manage risks to victims and the public, and make it possible to manage some people outside custody.

how-it-works.text: A curfew tag checks whether someone is at a specified address during set hours. Location tags can check a wider set of conditions, such as whether someone entered an exclusion zone. Alcohol tags detect alcohol through the skin.

how-it-came-to-be.text: The National Audit Office documented home fitting in 2013. The curfew service paired an ankle tag with a monitoring unit at the person’s address. The current service went live under new contracts in May 2024. In October 2026, changes under the Sentencing Act introduced a presumption of tagging for eligible prison leavers under the new release arrangements.

how-it-came-to-be.heading: Why weren’t tags fitted at the prison gate?
how-it-came-to-be.text: Asked about the old approach by the Public Accounts Committee, probation director general Jim Barton said most people with a tag also need a unit calibrated at their address. Fitting the tag during that home visit saved a visit. Fitting it in prison usually adds a second visit, and officials used the pilot to test the costs of doing both.

In October 2025 the Ministry piloted fitting before release in six prisons so monitoring could begin as people left. The current contract calls for prison visits when a fitting is required, with Serco responsible for staffing them.

in-numbers.text: Fewer people in the post-release group had equipment in September than in June. At the same time, the share without equipment rose from 12.8% to 13.9%. More people were recorded as in custody and without equipment in September (526) than in June (334).

scrutiny.text: The Public Accounts Committee questioned Ministry of Justice and prison and probation officials on 26 November 2026. These exchanges show what MPs tested, what officials said and what evidence would show progress. The summaries are based on the hearing recording.

outcomes.text: The Ministry of Justice compared people in its GPS pilot for eligible prison leavers with theft, burglary or other acquisitive offences with matched eligible people outside the pilot. It looked at new offences and at compliance with supervision as distinct outcomes.

outcomes.heading: Curfews on community orders
outcomes.text: A separate study in England and Wales compared people given an electronically monitored curfew as part of a community order with a matched group. Estimated reconviction for offences committed in the first 83 days was 17% versus 22%. People given a monitored curfew also received fewer warnings for breaking probation requirements and were more likely to complete other requirements during the order. This study assessed the monitored curfew as part of the sentence.

outcomes.heading: What happened while people waited for a tag?
outcomes.text: The national monitoring tables show equipment status at month end. The missing link is how many breaches or proven new offences occurred while monitoring was due but inactive. Tagging can also make a breach easier to detect, so comparing recorded breach totals alone can give a misleading picture of behaviour.

fitting-figures.question: How often do fittings succeed, and why is 15% unmonitored considered tolerable?
fitting-figures.answer: Officials said updated fitting figures would be published in January. Permanent Secretary Jo Farrar said the 15% threshold applies to a snapshot of people with an active monitoring order and can include people facing short waits. The audit had found that 45% of adult tag requests in 2025 and 62% in January to April 2026 led to a fitting within two attempts.
fitting-figures.watch: Compare the January figures with the audit using the same definition. Alongside the share unmonitored at a point in time, check how long each release cohort waits for monitoring to start.

followUp.title: Updated figures on successful fittings within two attempts

history.text: Officials said they would publish the figures in January 2027.

serco-payments.question: Can Serco meet its target or get paid when a tag goes unfitted?
serco-payments.answer: Jim Barton corrected his earlier evidence. Serco receives no payment for the first two unsuccessful visits, and is paid for further visits if prison and probation officials commission them. The audit found that Serco met its 95% visit timeliness target in February 2026 and fitted tags within those two attempts for 62% of the people it visited.
serco-payments.watch: Check which payments depend on fitting a tag, and whether the contract measures successful fittings as well as timely attempts.

followUp.title: Written explanation of Serco’s payment rules and target

history.text: The chair asked for a note before the committee prepared its report.

fittings-at-release.question: Why weren’t tags fitted before people left prison?
fittings-at-release.answer: Barton said the old model combined fitting the tag and setting up the monitoring unit in one home visit. The pilot tested the cost of fitting in prison and then visiting the address. The Ministry had announced an expansion to 83 prisons by the end of March 2027 the day before the hearing.
fittings-at-release.watch: As new prisons join, compare the share of eligible leavers with working monitoring at release and how long the rest wait. Count prisons for rollout coverage and follow release cohorts to see whether the change closes the gap.

out-of-hours.question: Who acts on a domestic abuse exclusion-zone breach outside office hours?
out-of-hours.answer: Sarah Olney asked whether a victim could be left waiting overnight. Barton said a small group on enhanced monitoring gets near-instant notifications while most cases follow the ordinary timetable. A notification still needs someone to assess the risk and act.
out-of-hours.watch: Look for elapsed time from breach to protective action, including how often police or probation acted and whether responses differ overnight or at weekends. Track enhanced and ordinary monitoring separately.

prompt-fitting.label: GPS or curfew tags fitted promptly
prompt-fitting.basis: Inspectors judged how promptly fitting took place in each case. About one in five individuals in the sample waited more than 14 days for GPS or curfew equipment.
prompt-fitting.population: Relevant GPS or curfew-tag cases in the inspection sample of community sentences and post-release licences
prompt-fitting.period: People sentenced or released September to November 2025

bail-breach-follow-through.label: Court bail cases with every response step recorded
bail-breach-follow-through.basis: Inspectors looked for a record of four steps: receiving the alert, assessing risk, making a decision and updating the monitoring service.
bail-breach-follow-through.population: 21 court bail breach cases reviewed in Lancashire and West Yorkshire

fitting-delay.title: Monitoring can start late or fail to start
fitting-delay.text: Inspectors found delays when a person was unavailable or when information needed to arrange the fitting was missing or wrong. Unstable accommodation can make home fitting harder. A provider can meet its contractual target by attempting a visit on time even when the fitting does not go ahead. The September figures also show why it matters to check that installed equipment is communicating.

improvement.title: Fit tags before eligible prison leavers leave custody
improvement.status: Six-prison pilot. On 25 November 2026 the Ministry announced expansion to 16 prisons in December, 50 in January 2027 and 83 by the end of March 2027.
improvement.measure: For each month’s prison leavers with a monitoring requirement, track the share with working equipment at release and by 24 hours, 48 hours and seven days. Link fitting dates to the dates of confirmed breaches, recalls and proven new offences to see what happened during the wait.
improvement.evidenceGap: The September snapshot predates the October release reforms. Evaluating the rollout needs comparable groups followed from release, with incidents dated to when they occurred and proven reoffending reported once follow-up is complete.

consequences.text: In one case, an exclusion zone meant to protect identified people went unmonitored for 41 days after a person left prison. Once monitoring started, it detected entries into the zone and enforcement followed. The inspectors documented those entries after activation.

In a historical case from 2003, a person subject to a monitored curfew took part in a fatal robbery while their tag was awaiting refitting. The inquiry also found that the monitoring provider had failed to pass on earlier evidence of curfew breaches.

alert-response.title: An alert needs someone to act on it
alert-response.text: The National Audit Office found that police and probation staff often lacked the information or capacity to respond quickly. Inspectors looking specifically at court bail found avoidable delays in some cases and incomplete records of what happened after a notification.

improvement.title: Improve records of what happens after a court bail alert
improvement.status: The Ministry partly accepted the recommendation to publish more detail. Its October action plan targets March 2027 for completing a data quality review.
improvement.measure: Track the share of notifications with a recorded risk assessment and enforcement decision, and how long those decisions take.
improvement.evidenceGap: The inspection sample provides a starting point. A consistent national series would make it possible to track progress across forces.

consequences.text: In a stalking case, police received repeated reports of apparent exclusion-zone breaches and the victim later reported further stalking. The defendant was eventually jailed for stalking. Inspectors found no record of a police risk assessment in the case.
